messages.content: I want to go to whistler for skiing. Can you give me the 5 day forecast for both the top and bottom of the mountain.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve data. This function is commonly used for API calls and web scraping. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The Date Nager API provides access holiday information for over 100 countries, including the ability to query for long weekends. It leverages ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes to tailor the search to your specific region of interest. More information can be found in https://date.nager.at/Api

headers.description: Optional headers to send with the request as a dictionary of header values.

Content-Type.description: The media type of the resource being requested, typically 'application/json'.

Authorization.description: The credentials to authenticate a user agent with a server, typically formatted as 'Bearer {token}'.

timeout.description: The maximum amount of time to wait for a response from the server, in seconds. A longer timeout may be necessary for slower network connections or overloaded servers. This is a float type value.

params.description: URL parameters to append to the URL. Sent as a dictionary of key-value pairs.

query.description: The query parameter for search or filtering.

page.description: The page number parameter for pagination. Used to retrieve a specific page of results.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials formatted as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem), if required for the request.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names and values.

sessionid.description: Session identifier cookie, used to recognize client sessions on the server.

csrftoken.description: CSRF protection token cookie, used to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary, mapping protocol or protocol and hostname to the URL of the proxy.

http.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTP requests, including the port number.

https.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTPS requests, including the port number.

stream.description: Whether to stream the download of the response. If False, the response content will be immediately downloaded. Streaming is useful for handling large files or responses.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not. Set to False to skip certificate verification, which is not recommended unless you are sure of the server's identity.

The user wants weather forecasts for Whistler ski area – specifically top and bottom of the mountain. We need to provide a 5-day forecast. Likely we should fetch weather data via an API like openweathermap or other. But no tool defined except requests_get; but we don't have direct knowledge of endpoints.

We could call some public API? For example, open-meteo.com offers free weather APIs without auth. Let's see: open-meteo has endpoint: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=...&longitude=...&hourly=temperature_2m etc. They also support daily precipitation probability, temperature max/min, wind speed, cloud cover, etc. That might suffice.

But we need location coordinates for Whistler Ski Resort. Latitude ~50.1138°N, longitude -122.9579°W. Top vs bottom difference maybe altitude differences. Could approximate using same lat/lon but different elevation param? Some APIs allow specifying elevation. Not all do. Alternatively, we can just note that top-of-mountain conditions differ due to higher elevation leading to lower temperatures and more snowfall. Provide separate predictions based on typical lapse rate (~6°C per km). Use base at 1200 m vs summit at 2000+ m. So adjust accordingly.

Thus produce forecast table for each day: high temp, low temp, chance of snow, wind speed, precipitation. Provide two sets: Bottom (approx 1300m?) and Top (approx 1900m?). We'll compute adjusted temps.

Ok too many. Instead choose simpler set: temperature_max, temperature_min, precipitation_probability_sum, snowfall_sum, windspeed_10m_max, cloudcover_total, sunshine hours perhaps.

Open-Meteo supports daily variable list limited to certain ones. According to docs: daily variables include: temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min, apparent_temperature_max, apparent_temperature_min, precipitation_sum, rainfall_sum, snowfall_sum, sunhours, sunrise, sunset, moonrise, moonset, ... Also windgusts_10m_max, winddirection_10m_dominant, windspeed_10m_avg, windspeed_10m_max, etc. Cloudcover_total, cloudcover_low, cloudcover_mid, cloudcover_high, shortwave_radiation_sum, etc.

So let's pick: temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min, precipitation_sum, snowfall_sum, windspeed_10m_max, cloudcover_total, sunhours.

Now we need to call open-meteo API. Format: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=50.1138&longitude=-122.9579&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min,sunshine_minutes,precipitation_sum,rainfall_sum,snowfall_sum,windspeed_10m_max,cloudcover_total&timezone=America/Vancouver

Also specify start_date and end_date? By default returns next days up to 7 days. Might return 7 days starting today. That's fine.

Then parse JSON.

After retrieving, we'll create tables for bottom and top. Adjust top temps downward by about 6°C per km times height diff. Suppose bottom at 1400m, top at 2100m -> diff 700m -> drop 4.2°C. Similarly adjust precipitation probabilities? Snowfall likely increases slightly. We'll add fudge factor: increase snowfall sum by +20% and reduce precipitation sum by similar proportion because it's mostly snow.

Wind speeds may increase slightly at higher altitudes; add 10%.

Cloud cover remains similar.

Sunshine minutes may decrease slightly.

Alternatively, we can present raw forecast plus notes explaining adjustments.

Better approach: Show raw forecast then show estimated top-of-mountain forecast after applying adjustment factors.

Will need to convert units: Temperature in Celsius already. Precipitation sums mm. Wind speed km/h. Sunlight minutes.

For readability, format nicely.

Edge cases: None.

1. Call open-meteo API via requests_get.

2. Parse JSON into dict.

3. Extract arrays for dates and each variable.

4. Build DataFrame-like structure manually.

5. Compute adjusted top-of-mountain values.

6. Output markdown tables.

Potential issues: open-meteo may require CORS? It's okay.
